concepts.name: Ecosystem Components
concepts.summary: Name and distinguish the living (biotic) and non-living (abiotic) parts of an ecosystem and how they form a community.

concepts.name: Producers, Consumers, Decomposers
concepts.summary: Explain how organisms are classed by how they obtain energy and what role each plays in an ecosystem.

concepts.name: Food Chains
concepts.summary: Describe and draw a food chain showing energy passing from producer to successive consumers, with arrows showing direction of energy flow.

concepts.name: Habitat and Niche
concepts.summary: Distinguish a habitat as where an organism lives from a niche as its role and resource use there.

concepts.name: Major Biomes
concepts.summary: Recall the main biomes such as tundra, desert, grassland, forest and ocean and their typical climate and organisms.

concepts.name: Water Cycle Stages
concepts.summary: Explain evaporation, condensation, precipitation and runoff as a continuous movement of water through ecosystems.

concepts.name: Population and Community
concepts.summary: Define population, community, ecosystem and biosphere and place examples at the right level.

misconceptions.text: Arrows in a food chain show who eats whom rather than the direction energy flows.
Decomposers are not really part of the food chain and are unimportant to ecosystems.
A habitat and a niche are the same thing.

concepts.name: Trophic Levels
concepts.summary: Assign organisms to primary, secondary and tertiary trophic levels, recognising that omnivores can occupy more than one.

concepts.name: Food Webs
concepts.summary: Construct and read a food web to predict how removing or adding a species affects others.

concepts.name: Energy Pyramids
concepts.summary: Apply the roughly 10% transfer rule to calculate energy available at each level and explain why chains are short.

concepts.name: Predator-Prey Relationships
concepts.summary: Describe how predator and prey numbers rise and fall together in linked cycles.

concepts.name: Competition and Symbiosis
concepts.summary: Classify interactions as competition, mutualism, commensalism or parasitism and give examples.

concepts.name: Population Growth Patterns
concepts.summary: Interpret J-shaped and S-shaped growth curves and identify the carrying capacity on a graph.

concepts.name: Nitrogen Cycle Steps
concepts.summary: Trace nitrogen through fixation, nitrification, assimilation, ammonification and denitrification and name the organisms involved.

concepts.name: Primary and Secondary Succession
concepts.summary: Distinguish succession starting on bare rock from that following disturbance of existing soil.

misconceptions.text: Removing one species from a food web only affects the species that directly eat it or are eaten by it.
The missing 90% of energy between trophic levels is destroyed.
Predators always reduce prey populations to the detriment of the prey species.

concepts.name: Productivity and Energy Efficiency
concepts.summary: Calculate net primary productivity from gross productivity and respiration and compare transfer efficiencies between levels.

concepts.name: Lotka-Volterra Dynamics
concepts.summary: Analyse lagged oscillations of predator and prey and the assumptions that underlie the simple model.

concepts.name: Competitive Exclusion and Niche Partitioning
concepts.summary: Analyse how species with overlapping niches either exclude one another or coexist by dividing resources.

concepts.name: Density-Dependent Regulation
concepts.summary: Distinguish density-dependent from density-independent limiting factors and explain how they shape logistic growth.

concepts.name: Life History Strategies
concepts.summary: Compare r-selected and K-selected species and relate traits to environment stability and population dynamics.

concepts.name: Diversity Measurement
concepts.summary: Calculate and interpret species richness and diversity indices from sample data.

concepts.name: Mechanisms of Succession
concepts.summary: Analyse how pioneer species change conditions, how facilitation and inhibition operate, and why climax is not a fixed endpoint.

concepts.name: Biogeochemical Cycle Reservoirs
concepts.summary: Compare carbon, nitrogen and phosphorus cycles by their reservoirs, fluxes and human disturbances.

misconceptions.text: Competition between species always ends with one species eliminating the other.
Populations stay fixed at carrying capacity once they reach it.
A diverse community is simply one with many species, regardless of how evenly individuals are distributed.

concepts.name: Trophic Cascades and Keystone Species
concepts.summary: Analyse how keystone predators and top-down effects restructure communities, as in wolves in Yellowstone or sea otters and kelp.

concepts.name: Top-Down Versus Bottom-Up Control
concepts.summary: Evaluate evidence for whether resources or consumers limit community structure in a given ecosystem.

concepts.name: Metapopulations and Habitat Fragmentation
concepts.summary: Analyse how patch size, isolation and dispersal affect persistence and species richness.

concepts.name: Intermediate Disturbance and Diversity
concepts.summary: Evaluate how disturbance frequency and intensity shape diversity and when the intermediate disturbance hypothesis holds.

concepts.name: Population Viability Analysis
concepts.summary: Use age-structured models and stochasticity to judge a population's extinction risk and the weight of management options.

concepts.name: Ecosystem Stability and Resilience
concepts.summary: Assess resistance, resilience and tipping points, including regime shifts such as clear to turbid lakes.

concepts.name: Nutrient Loading and Eutrophication
concepts.summary: Analyse how fertiliser runoff alters nutrient cycling, drives algal blooms and oxygen depletion, and propagates through food webs.

concepts.name: Bioaccumulation and Biomagnification
concepts.summary: Explain how persistent pollutants concentrate up trophic levels and predict which organisms are most exposed.

misconceptions.text: A keystone species is simply the most abundant species in a community.
Ecosystems respond to stress gradually and reversibly, so removing the stressor restores the original state.
Disturbance is always harmful to biodiversity.

concepts.name: Coexistence Theory Evaluation
concepts.summary: Evaluate stabilising versus equalising mechanisms and neutral models as explanations of species coexistence against empirical data.

concepts.name: Biodiversity-Ecosystem Function Debate
concepts.summary: Judge experimental evidence on how diversity affects productivity and stability, separating complementarity from selection effects.

concepts.name: Experimental Design in Ecology
concepts.summary: Design field and mesocosm studies with proper replication, controls and scale to address confounding and pseudoreplication.

concepts.name: Early Warning Signals of Collapse
concepts.summary: Evaluate statistical indicators of approaching tipping points and the limits of their reliability.

concepts.name: Network Structure and Stability
concepts.summary: Assess how connectance, modularity, interaction strength and nestedness influence the stability of food webs and mutualistic networks.

concepts.name: Ecological Forecasting Models
concepts.summary: Build and critique models projecting population and range responses to climate change, accounting for uncertainty and model assumptions.

concepts.name: Ecosystem Management and Restoration Design
concepts.summary: Create restoration or conservation plans that integrate succession, trophic and nutrient dynamics and weigh trade-offs and uncertainty.

concepts.name: Scale and Context Dependence
concepts.summary: Evaluate how patterns and generalisations change with spatial and temporal scale and reconcile conflicting results across studies.

misconceptions.text: More species always means a more stable and productive ecosystem in every context.
Early warning indicators reliably predict every regime shift in advance.
Findings from a small plot experiment can be applied directly to whole landscapes.
